EarthTrend Detective

Case #001 — Jharkhand

Generated: 2026-10-12 09:22 UTC

Evidence status: PASS

Executive Summary

Across the analyzed Jharkhand SMAP record, no statistically significant long-term monotonic soil-moisture decline was detected. The state-level trend was slightly negative but highly non-significant, and none of the 984 SMAP cells had a statistically significant long-term trend in the first-pass cell analysis. Seasonal analysis also found no significant state-level seasonal trends, while the seven raw significant cell-season results disappeared after Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction, leaving no statistically robust spatial-seasonal hotspots. At the same time, the record contains widespread episodic soil-moisture extremes. Soil-moisture and rainfall anomalies show a strong positive same-month association, and that overall association remains significant after an autocorrelation-aware effective-sample-size adjustment. The spatial rainfall relationship is also consistently positive across the mapped SMAP cells and remains stable when the analysis is restricted to closer SMAP-GPM matches. Together, the evidence supports strong rainfall-linked variability and episodic extremes, rather than a simple state-wide long-term drying claim.

Scientific caution: Association does not establish causation. Interpret conclusions within the documented data coverage, methods, and limitations.

Scientific Methodology

Study coverage and data alignment

Monthly NASA SMAP soil-moisture observations cover Jharkhand from April 2015 through September 2026. The NASA GPM IMERG rainfall comparison covers the common period April 2015 through September 2025. SMAP cells are matched to nearby GPM grid cells. The datasets have different spatial resolutions, and matched observations are not fully independent.

Trend analysis

Sen's slope summarizes trend magnitude, and a Kendall/Mann–Kendall-style test evaluates monotonic trend evidence. Seasonal and cell-level results are examined separately. The Benjamini–Hochberg false-discovery-rate procedure is used for documented multiple-comparison analyses.

Extreme-event screening

Standardized soil-moisture anomalies screen unusually dry and wet cell-months. A candidate month requires at least 5% of the 984 cells (50 or more cells) to reach z ≤ −2 for dry conditions or z ≥ +2 for wet conditions. These are screening definitions, not proof of impacts or causes.

Rainfall association

Pearson correlation measures linear association between standardized rainfall and soil-moisture anomalies; Spearman correlation provides a rank-based comparison. Lagged and seasonal associations are also examined. An effective-sample-size adjustment addresses temporal autocorrelation in the reported overall rainfall association. Correlation does not establish causality.

Interpretation safeguards

A non-significant trend does not prove that no change occurred. The primary trend test is not a fully seasonality- and autocorrelation-corrected trend model, and the seasonal analysis is not a fully autocorrelation-corrected Seasonal Mann–Kendall implementation. Spatial dependence, grid-resolution differences, small seasonal samples, and event-threshold choices limit interpretation. This report reproduces saved evidence; it does not recalculate statistical results.

Final FindingAcross the analyzed Jharkhand SMAP record, no statistically significant long-term monotonic soil-moisture decline was detected. The state-level trend was slightly negative but highly non-significant, and none of the 984 SMAP cells had a statistically significant long-term trend in the first-pass cell analysis. Seasonal analysis also found no significant state-level seasonal trends, while the seven raw significant cell-season results disappeared after Benjamini-Hochberg FDR correction, leaving no statistically robust spatial-seasonal hotspots. At the same time, the record contains widespread episodic soil-moisture extremes. Soil-moisture and rainfall anomalies show a strong positive same-month association, and that overall association remains significant after an autocorrelation-aware effective-sample-size adjustment. The spatial rainfall relationship is also consistently positive across the mapped SMAP cells and remains stable when the analysis is restricted to closer SMAP-GPM matches. Together, the evidence supports strong rainfall-linked variability and episodic extremes, rather than a simple state-wide long-term drying claim.
Causality StatementThe analyses demonstrate association, not causality.

Limitations

Item 1The primary long-term SMAP trend test is a first-pass Kendall/Mann-Kendall-style analysis and is not a fully seasonality- and autocorrelation-corrected trend model.
Item 2The seasonal trend analysis explicitly states that it is not an autocorrelation-corrected Seasonal Mann-Kendall implementation.
Item 3Seasonal rainfall-soil-moisture analyses use relatively small complete season-year sample sizes; therefore seasonal estimates should be interpreted cautiously.
Item 4The GPM comparison period ends in September 2025, whereas the SMAP analysis continues through September 2026.
Item 5The spatial cross-variable analysis maps 984 SMAP cells to 703 coarser GPM cells, so the 984 spatial correlations are not 984 independent spatial experiments.
Item 6FDR significance in the spatial cross-variable analysis is a multiple-testing screening result and does not remove all spatial-dependence concerns.
Item 7Extreme-event thresholds and the minimum 5 percent affected-cell criterion are analytical definitions used by this study.
Item 8Correlation and lagged association establish statistical association, not physical causality.
